units.text: We'll decide if an AI release is ready by comparing the evidence. Freeze the representative test inputs. Run the baseline and candidate through the same evaluation so a change in score is more likely to reflect the release, not a different test set.

Check the metrics, reviewer judgments and predefined release thresholds. Block a candidate if it misses a required guardrail. Preserve what was tested and monitor actual use after release. One good score isn't a production guarantee.

For a retrieval-augmented answer, first ask whether the retrieved passages were relevant and appropriate. Use known questions and difficult cases. If the source passage is wrong or missing, a fluent final answer does not fix retrieval.

Then inspect whether the response uses the evidence, answers correctly and handles unsafe or uncertain cases. Review ambiguous cases with a person. Keep the artifacts and system versions so the next evaluation can compare the same conditions.

We'll follow a container from a tooling account to production. Build a pinned revision, scan the resulting image and attach evidence to that digest. Promote the digest, not a tag that could point to something else later.

Approval authorizes the identified release. The production deployment uses a scoped role, and its actions must be authorized to consume the artifact. Monitor the canary and verify the running digest after promotion.

The new version receives the canary share. Errors rise and a configured CloudWatch alarm trips. CodeDeploy follows the configured rollback and stops sending new traffic to the failing version. Confirm the prior version is healthy before retrying.

If the failing version already wrote data, restoring traffic doesn't reverse those writes. Check the data effects and use an appropriate recovery plan. Repair the cause and validate before attempting another release.

We'll follow a slow checkout request and ask which dependency accounts for the delay. The service map shows separate payment and inventory paths. The sample duration makes payments the first dependency to investigate, not automatically the root cause.

Use metrics to see whether the delay repeats, logs to understand a request outcome, and a trace to see where that request spent time. The topology tells you where to look; the telemetry shows what happened.

A metric puts a number on change over time, such as increasing latency or error rate. That tells you when symptoms started and whether they are broad, but it usually doesn't show the exact failing request.
Look at a request trace to find the slow span, then match it to relevant logs for what happened in that service. A meaningful incident usually needs more than one type of evidence.

Namespace, metric name and dimension set identify the metric. The two Regions in this example are different series even though they report the same name. Query the identity actually published; omitting a custom dimension doesn't automatically merge its values.

If you need a combined view, select and aggregate the relevant series deliberately. Keep high-cardinality values such as a request identifier in logs or traces when appropriate. Otherwise you can create many distinct custom series and lose a useful comparison.

E C two publishes infrastructure metrics such as C P U and network activity. Guest memory and filesystem usage are different. Use an agent or equivalent guest instrumentation to publish those values, then query the resulting namespace and dimensions.
E B S volume metrics describe the storage system. They don't necessarily tell you how full the filesystem inside the instance is. Choose the signal that answers the operational question.

We'll evaluate an alarm from the actual data. In this example the threshold is eighty percent, with three breaching datapoints required out of five periods. The three readings above eighty are enough even though they aren't all consecutive.

A silent metric can mean healthy operation, missing telemetry or a service with intermittent events. Choose how to treat missing data based on what the signal normally does. Verify the alarm detects an intentional test without staying noisy during expected gaps.

The same alarm state can notify a person through S N S, request a scaling change, or invoke configured Lambda code. Choose the action based on the intended outcome, and give the action only the authority it needs.
Most alarm actions run on a state transition; Auto Scaling actions can repeat while the condition remains. Test the alarm and verify whether the configured outcome actually happened.
